title: Local DP telemetry (RAPPOR)
description: RAPPOR (Google) collects telemetry with local differential privacy: each client randomizes its report (Bloom filter + randomized response) before sending. The aggregator learns population statistics — '12% of users hit this crash' — while each individual report is deniable. Deployed in Chrome for years.
method: Encode value in a Bloom filter; randomize bits (randomized response); aggregate noisy reports; decode population statistics.
usage: Use for population statistics from untrusted collectors; tune the Bloom filter and randomization for your ε.

demo.code:
import random
random.seed(10)
reports = [1 if random.random() < 0.7 else 0 for _ in range(1000)]  # noisy
print(f'noisy reports suggest ~{sum(reports)/len(reports):.0%} (true 50%, denoised estimate)')

title: Private quantiles and histograms
description: Latency distributions, not just means: private histograms add Laplace noise per bucket, and private quantiles use the exponential mechanism over candidate values. 'p99 latency rose to 800ms' — learned from millions of devices, none identified.
method: Bucket the metric; add Laplace noise per bucket; derive quantiles; the noise hides individuals, the shape survives.
usage: Size buckets for your metric's range; more buckets = more noise total (budget split).

title: Secure aggregation (federated)
description: Secure aggregation (Bonawitz et al.) lets a server learn the sum of client values without seeing any individual one — masked contributions cancel out in aggregate. Federated learning uses it: the server improves the model from millions of phones while each phone's update stays private.
method: Clients mask updates with pairwise secrets; the server sums masked values; masks cancel; the server learns only the sum.
usage: Use for federated analytics/ML; handle dropouts (the protocol's hard part).

demo.code:
print('1M phones: masked gradient updates -> server sums')
print('server learns: aggregate gradient (no individual update visible)')

title: Differential privacy for dashboards
description: Internal dashboards query telemetry constantly; wrapping the dashboard backend in DP (per-query budgets, noisy results, cached answers) means employees explore freely without each query eroding privacy. The dashboard is the privacy boundary, not just a display.
method: DP query layer under dashboards; budget per analyst; cache noisy answers; the dashboard never sees raw data.
usage: Put DP under every internal telemetry dashboard; budget analysts like API rate limits.

demo.code:
print('dashboard: "crash rate by version" -> DP answer 2.3% ±0.1')
print('analyst budget: 4.1/10 spent today')

title: Telemetry data minimization
description: Collect the minimum that answers the question: crash stacks yes, full memory dumps no; feature usage counts yes, keystroke logs never. Minimization review precedes every new telemetry field — the cheapest privacy is data never collected.
method: Justify each field; prefer aggregates over raw; review new fields; expire aggressively.
usage: Challenge every new field; 'might be useful someday' is not a justification.

demo.code:
print('proposal: collect full URLs -> REJECTED (paths may contain tokens)')
print('approved: collect domain + status code (sufficient for the question)')

title: Transparency reports
description: Publish what telemetry exists, what it showed, and how privacy was protected — regular transparency reports build the trust that makes telemetry sustainable. What's collected, what's learned, what's spent: the public accounting of the private system.
method: Report collection, findings, and privacy spend regularly; make reports specific enough to verify.
usage: Publish on schedule; specificity is what makes reports credible.

demo.code:
print('Q3 telemetry report: 12 fields, eps spend 2.1, top finding: crash SIG-8812')
print('published: 2026-10-01 (verifiable claims)')

title: Aggregation service design
description: The collector architecture matters: separate ingestion (authenticated but immediately de-identified) from analysis (sees only aggregates), with retention limits between. Defense in depth for telemetry — even a compromised analyzer finds only aggregates, and raw reports auto-expire.
method: Ingest -> de-identify -> aggregate -> expire raw; the analyzer never sees raw reports; retention enforced automatically.
usage: Enforce the split architecturally (different services, different credentials); expire raw data aggressively.

demo.code:
print('ingest: 1M reports -> de-identified in 1h -> raw EXPIRED')
print('analyzer: aggregates only (raw unrecoverable)')

title: Opt-in and consent telemetry
description: The non-cryptographic foundation: telemetry is opt-in, consent is granular (crash reports yes, usage stats no), and users can inspect what's sent. No privacy mechanism substitutes for consent — the best systems combine honest consent UX with strong technical privacy.
method: Opt-in by default-off (or clear opt-out where appropriate); granular toggles; inspectable payloads; honor signals (GPC).
usage: Make consent real (not dark patterns); let users see exactly what's collected.

demo.code:
print('telemetry settings: [x] crash reports [ ] usage stats [ ] performance')
print('user inspects payload: {"crash": "SIG-8812", "os": "android-14"}')
